newsitem.title: UK: Oil prices move higher despite easing Iraq worry.
newsitem.headline: Oil prices move higher despite easing Iraq worry.

text.p: Oil prices firmed on Tuesday as the market continued to consolidate after tension in Iraq last week sent prices soaring to their highest levels since the Gulf War.
World benchmark Brent Blend crude oil from the North Sea was trading up nine cents at $22.70 a barrel on London's International Petroleum Exchange (IPE), having sunk to $22.32 earlier in the day.

In the absence of any fresh military action in Iraq, brokers said the fact prices had not broken through technical support levels on the downside was driving the price bounce. "It was a classic bounce," said one broker.
"We've managed to make some new highs and that's leading us up," said another.

Prices spiked up a dollar last week after Iraqi troops moved into Iraqi Kurdistan in support of a Kurdish faction, drawing U.S. retaliatory attacks against targets in the south of Iraq and prompting suspension of a U.N.-sponsored oil-for-food deal.
Iraq, whose exports have been under a United Nations embargo since it invaded Kuwait in August 1990, was to have been allowed limited oil sales to pay for essential food and medicines.
In anticipation of resumed Iraqi oil sales some refineries had allowed their stocks to run low and subsequently had to scramble to cover requirements at higher prices.
Since then the market has been consolidating at new higher levels and waiting for any fresh news out of the Middle East.
Prices have also been supported by renewed demand for gas oil (heating oil) ahead of the northern hemisphere winter.

With analysts fearing that low stocks of heating oil in both the United States and Europe might fall short of meeting winter demand, a close eye will be kept on heating stocks data out of the United States later on Wednesday.
"Without a build in heating oil, prices are likely to rise," said GNI in its daily energy report.
